GE Aerospace stock: Hybrid propulsion meets strong services demand
sum: GE Aerospace drew attention this week from two different angles: a hybrid-electric propulsion milestone and resilient demand for engine services. The developments strengthen the long-term technology story while highlighting the recurring revenue tied to aircraft already in operation.

On November 5, Aviation Week reported that GE Aerospace's modified Saab 340B successfully used electrically augmented power during takeoff. The test, conducted with BETA Technologies in Plattsburgh, New York, was described as the first hybrid-propulsion takeoff for an aircraft designed to operate at commercial airliner altitudes.

Initial observations indicated lower takeoff noise with hybrid power, although GE did not provide comparative noise measurements. The technology is part of work that could support future propulsion systems, including the CFM Open Fan technology demonstration under the GE Aerospace and Safran RISE program. The aircraft remains a test platform, with no announced certification or commercial entry timetable.

A separate Yahoo Finance report on November 6 highlighted GE Aerospace's latest operating momentum. Orders rose 49 percent to 19.0 billion US dollars in the latest quarter, while commercial segment revenue increased 21 percent and services revenue advanced 17 percent.

The report said management lifted 2026 adjusted EPS guidance to 8.00 to 8.10 US dollars from 7.65 to 7.85 US dollars. A services backlog above 170 billion US dollars and an installed base of more than 80,000 engines provide visibility as Boeing delivery delays encourage airlines to keep older aircraft flying longer.

sum: GE Aerospace stock is facing a changing aviation mix: Boeing production delays are limiting new-aircraft deliveries, while airlines continue operating older jets that require maintenance, spare parts and engine shop visits. A Yahoo Finance analysis by Harry Jones, published Thursday, November 5, said the shift is supporting GE Aerospace's services business. The article said its financial figures were current as of November 4.
GE Aerospace stock traded at 294.50 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 13:31 CET on Thursday, November 5, 2026; investors can follow the real-time quote of GE Aerospace stock.

The analysis reported that GE Aerospace orders rose 49 percent to 19.0 billion US dollars in the latest quarter and that the company raised its full-year outlook for a fourth consecutive quarter. Commercial segment revenue increased 21 percent year over year, while services revenue advanced 17 percent. Segment orders rose 58 percent, ahead of the companywide rate.

Adjusted operating profit increased 30 percent to 3.0 billion US dollars, producing a 22.5 percent margin after a 220-basis-point expansion, according to the report. Adjusted earnings per share reached 2.25 US dollars, up 36 percent year over year and above the cited 2.00 US dollar consensus estimate. Management lifted 2026 adjusted earnings-per-share guidance to 8.00 to 8.10 US dollars from 7.65 to 7.85 US dollars.

The installed base of more than 80,000 engines supports a services backlog above 170 billion US dollars. Services orders were up 30 percent during the year, and more than 95 percent of fourth-quarter spare-parts revenue was already covered by the backlog, the analysis said. That visibility may help cushion the business if aircraft production remains uneven.

Airlines are retiring CFM56 engines more slowly than previously expected. The report put the retirement rate at 1.5 to 2.0 percent, below an earlier 3.0 to 4.0 percent forecast. A longer service life for older aircraft can support parts demand and maintenance activity independently of new-aircraft deliveries.
At the same time, LEAP deliveries were up 26 percent year to date, while the LEAP and GEnx installed bases are expected to roughly double by 2030.

sum: GE Aerospace stock traded at 286.55 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 13:30:57 CET on Wednesday, November 4, 2026. The current focus is the company's hybrid-electric propulsion program, whose modified Saab 340B demonstrator has completed testing above 30,000 feet.

The aircraft was developed with NASA, BETA Technologies and Boeing through the Electrified Powertrain Flight Demonstration program. The test platform combines an electric powertrain with a conventional gas turbine, allowing GE Aerospace and its partners to assess propulsion integration under conditions closer to commercial flight.

The demonstrator has also completed a hybrid-electric flight lasting more than two hours. The program brings together motor-generators, power electronics, control systems, gearboxes, propellers and thermal-management equipment in one aircraft platform.

GE Aerospace executives have described the flight milestone as progress toward future propulsion systems. The company is considering possible applications across commercial, cargo and military aircraft, although the technology still requires further testing, scaling and certification before it could support regular passenger operations.

For investors, the development strengthens GE Aerospace's longer-term technology narrative but does not by itself provide a near-term earnings catalyst. Commercial deployment remains dependent on aircraft integration, system weight, reliability, safety and regulatory approval. Is GE Aerospace Stock Increasing Your Market Risk?
sum: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Investors holding GE Aerospace (GE) alongside an S&P 500 fund own a jet-engine maker that has increased sales from a year earlier in each of the last five quarters. A growing business can still produce a volatile stock, however, and your portfolio feels the stock’s movements rather than the company’s sales. So does owning GE make the market’s bad days worse for your money?

During the year ended October 30, 2026, a $10,000 holding in GE lost about $71.50 on the average day the S&P 500 fell, while the same sum in the index lost about $61. The difference was smaller on the market’s up days: the GE holding gained about $66 on the average up day, compared with about $63 in the index.

Over the same year, GE posted a beta of 1.23, a metric measuring how far the stock moves for each 1% move in the index. Beta is calculated from all daily movements combined over the year, so it captures something different from the up-day and down-day averages above. The stock’s volatility, a measure of how widely the price swings over a year, was 33.5%, against 12.8% for the S&P 500. For an investment portfolio, this means GE adds to existing market risk rather than offsetting it, and it adds more on the way down than on the way up.

Closely. GE’s commercial engines and services business accounted for $33.3 billion of the company’s $45.9 billion in fiscal 2025 revenue. On the company’s October 20, 2026 call, management said airline departures are the main source of demand for its services.

Over the past year, GE’s daily moves tracked the S&P 500 only loosely. The correlation between the two was 0.47, where 1 would mean moving in step, so a large part of GE’s day-to-day movement was its own.

Management raised its 2026 guidance on that call and expects low double-digit growth in commercial services in 2027. Still, most of GE’s sales come from a single business tied to how much airlines fly, operating in an environment management itself calls dynamic.

Over its latest four quarters, GE Aerospace (GE) grew faster and earned a wider operating margin than each of the four peers in its group with comparable figures. Honeywell’s figures are distorted by its 2026 spin-off of its aerospace business. The stock trades at the highest P/E of the six, yet shares returned less over the past year than three of those peers. How far ahead of its peers is GE’s business, and how much more are you paying for it?

GE grew revenue 19.6% over its latest four quarters and produced an 18.2% operating margin. RTX, its largest peer by market value, posted 11.6% revenue growth and an 11.8% operating margin over the same period. Buying into that lead requires paying 35.6 times GE’s earnings, against 32.1 times for RTX.

Lockheed Martin and Northrop Grumman also grew more slowly and trade at lower P/Es than GE. The industrial conglomerate Honeywell is excluded from the group’s P/E ranking because it reported a net loss in its quarter ended December 31, 2025, one of its latest four.
GE’s shares have failed to match that lead. Including dividends, the stock returned 1.6% over the year to October 29, 2026, against 13.3% for RTX.

Jim Cramer Is “Sick and Tired” of Diversifying Into Stocks That Aren’t That Good
sum: Jim Cramer went on live television and called out one of investing's most sacred rules, and the morning's earnings reports gave him some uncomfortable ammunition to work with.

Jim Cramer started Wednesday by pushing back on one of investing’s oldest rules. On CNBC the morning of October 28, 2026, as GE Vernova (NYSE:GEV | GEV Price Prediction) and GE HealthCare (NASDAQ:GEHC) both reported third-quarter results, he said: “I am sick and tired of people saying you’ve got to be diversified into things that aren’t that good. Okay, maybe you get lucky with GE HealthCare today, but these companies are great companies that are doing really well. And we turned on them; we turned on them. And I find myself thinking, what am I turning to?”
His point: if your best companies keep delivering, selling them to buy weaker businesses just to spread your money around can drag down your returns.

Cramer pointed to gas turbines. Cramer said GE Vernova gas turbine orders rose from 7.4 gigawatts in the third quarter of 2025 to 16.6 gigawatts in the third quarter of 2026. The company’s third-quarter release backs up his point. Revenue rose 26.4% to $12.60B, and orders reached $29.30B, up 96% organically. Backlog hit $197.00B, and management expects it to exceed $200B in the fourth quarter. Gas equipment backlog plus slot reservations rose to 122 GW. Free cash flow guidance went up to $16-$17B. The stock is up 35.71% year-to-date.

The “we turned on them” line matches the rest of his list. GE Aerospace (NYSE:GE) made $2.25 per share in adjusted EPS against a $1.99 consensus, reported orders up 49%, and raised full-year EPS guidance to $8.00-$8.10. Even so, its shares are down 1.25% year-to-date. Constellation Energy (NASDAQ:CEG) raised 2026 EPS guidance to $11.50-$12.50, yet the stock is down 26.71% this year. Vistra (NYSE:VST) reported Ongoing Operations Adjusted EBITDA up more than 30%, but its stock fell 10.71%.

He named GE HealthCare as the stock that got lucky. It beat with adjusted EPS of $1.34 against $1.20 expected and rose 7.94% in Wednesday trading. It is still down 6.22% year to date, and its full-year organic growth guidance is only about 4.0%.

Why Is Boeing Stock Falling While Revenue Soars Past Peers?
sum: Boeing (BA) grew revenue faster over the past twelve months than any of its aerospace and defense peers, GE Aerospace included, and its stock still fell. It is also the only one in that group running an operating loss. The growth has come with rising airplane deliveries, and the market is waiting to see whether those airplanes earn a margin.

GE Aerospace is the sharpest comparison. It grew revenue 21.7% over the trailing twelve months, close to Boeing’s 24.8%, on an operating margin of 18.7%, and its stock returned 13.4%. Boeing’s operating margin over the same twelve months was negative 5.4%. Its stock returned negative 4.4%.

Nearly the same growth, opposite margins, opposite returns. RTX grew revenue less than half as fast as Boeing, and its stock returned 25.7%. The market is paying GE Aerospace and RTX for the profit on each sale, and Boeing is the only company in the group with no operating profit to show.

Management has pointed to long-standing supply chain architecture as a primary factor dictating how margins are distributed between airframers and component suppliers on current delivery programs. Boeing is managing supplier bottlenecks on 787 engine deliveries, which lagged in the first half of 2026 and constrain the ramp from eight to ten aircraft per month. While suppliers maintain healthier margins, Boeing carries the integration and delivery burden.

Commercial Airplanes still lost money on operations in the June 2026 quarter despite handing over 171 airplanes, its most since 2018, though its margin improved from a year earlier on the higher volume.

The CFO says program cash margins on the 737 and 787 sit only slightly above breakeven, held down largely by a pricing drag that fades as deliveries climb and better-priced backlog comes through. The 737 is ramping to 47 airplanes per month. Volume is arriving before the margin does.

Cash is the scoreboard. Management guides 2026 free cash flow to $1 billion to $3 billion, on a record backlog of $715 billion. That backlog is more than seven years of revenue at the trailing pace of $94.0 billion, so demand is not the doubt. Landing inside the 2026 range says the deliveries are turning into cash. Missing it says the pricing drag is still eating the volume.

Howmet Aerospace (HWM) Faces New Competitive Pressure after GE’s $11.75 Billion CPP Deal
sum: Howmet Aerospace Inc. (NYSE:HWM) is facing a mixed outlook after GE Aerospace agreed to acquire Consolidated Precision Products (CPP) for about $11.75 billion to secure more control over critical engine castings and expand production capacity. The announcement initially hit Howmet shares, which fell about 10%, as investors worried that GE could eventually rely less on outside suppliers such as Howmet.

However, Howmet CEO John Plant said he is comfortable with the deal and remains confident in Howmet's ability to grow. The bigger issue for Howmet right now appears to be how quickly it can expand capacity to keep up with soaring demand. Commercial aircraft production, defense activity and aftermarket demand are all increasing, while Howmet is also benefiting from demand for turbine components used in data centers. Plant said the scale of the required capital expansion is itself "testing" the company.
Howmet's Growth Opportunity Remains Intact Despite GE's Move

The strongest bullish argument for Howmet Aerospace Inc. (NYSE:HWM) is that GE's decision to spend nearly $12 billion on CPP validates how strategically valuable aerospace castings and engine components have become. The acquisition is aimed at addressing a supply bottleneck rather than signaling weak demand. GE expects airfoil demand to rise by more than 30% through 2030, while aircraft manufacturers and defense customers continue to push production higher. That creates a favorable industry backdrop for Howmet as well.

Howmet also has an opportunity to benefit from customers looking for additional capacity outside GE's newly integrated supply chain. If demand continues to exceed available casting capacity, Howmet's existing manufacturing footprint and expertise could give it significant pricing power and support further investment. Plant's comments that the company is being "tested" by the sheer scale of expansion suggest that Howmet is dealing with a capacity problem caused by strong demand, rather than a lack of orders.

Another positive is that Howmet Aerospace Inc. (NYSE:HWM)'s exposure extends beyond commercial aircraft. Its blades and vanes are also used in gas turbines serving the rapidly expanding data-center market, providing another avenue for growth alongside aerospace.

items.t: GE Aerospace Stock Is Priced For A Margin Repair That Has Not Happened Yet
sum: The engines it is shipping to build tomorrow’s service revenue are costing margin today, and the shares carry almost no cushion if that bill runs long.

GE Aerospace (GE) has delivered strong shareholder returns. The stock trades at $356.23, up 33.4% over the past year against 20.6% for the S&P 500. The biggest risk to it now is not demand, which is running ahead of what the company can ship. It is that the price already assumes a repair the company’s own timetable does not deliver until 2028 at the earliest.
Management Expects The Margin Bill For Growth To Peak By 2028

The margin compression is expected, by the company’s own account, and it carries a date. In Q2 2026, Commercial Engines & Services margin fell 160 basis points to 27.3%, which management attributed to installed engine growth, including GE9X investments, and inflation. The GE9X units going out now are the initial, highest-cost ones, and management expects those losses to peak by 2028, the same point at which it expects LEAP services margins to come into line with its total services portfolio. Even with these pressures, management says total-company margins are largely flat. Every engine shipped today builds a service annuity that pays later and costs margin now.

The second risk is the company’s own ability to ship. Spare parts delinquencies, which are shipments delayed by material availability, grew 20% sequentially in Q2 2026, even as spare parts sales rose more than 25% year-over-year. By management’s own account the constraint is supply, not demand. That caps how fast orders turn into revenue. None of this makes GE Aerospace a weak business: its net margin of 17.7% and revenue growth of 21.7% are among the highest of its closest peers. Quality of that kind is what the Trefis High Quality Portfolio looks for in a holding.

GE Aerospace’s price-to-earnings multiple is among the lowest of its closest peers, which is the usual rebuttal to any valuation worry. The trouble is that peers are the wrong yardstick for valuation: what matters is what this business is worth against every earlier version of itself.

The T901 Engine Clears Its First Flight Gate
sum: It is not often that an aircraft gets fifty percent more power without getting any bigger. That is exactly what the U.S. Army is trying to bolt into thousands of its helicopters — and on 12 August 2026 the effort passed one of its hardest gates. GE Aerospace's T901-GE-900 turboshaft, the new engine at the centre of the Army's Improved Turbine Engine Program, cleared its Preliminary Flight Rating.

In plain terms: the engine is now judged safe to fly on a test aircraft. It is the step that turns a machine that has run for hundreds of hours on a test stand into one that will actually leave the ground bolted to a Black Hawk.
The number that matters is 1,000. That is how many extra shaft horsepower the T901 adds over the engine it replaces — and it does it in the same space, at almost the same weight.

The engineering trick of the T901 is restraint. The Army did not want a new engine that forced a new airframe; it wanted a drop-in replacement that fits the existing nacelle of the Apache and the Black Hawk. GE's answer is a single-spool core — simpler than the twin-spool T700 it supersedes — combined with additive-manufactured parts and ceramic-matrix-composite components that survive higher turbine temperatures. More heat, handled cleanly, means more power from the same volume of air.

The result is roughly 3,000 shaft horsepower against the T700's 2,000, plus a quarter better fuel burn, in a package the same size and weight. That margin is not a luxury. The Black Hawk and Apache have both gained weight steadily since the 1970s as radios, armour, sensors and weapons piled on. The T901 gives that heavier fleet back its climb rate, its hot-and-high performance, and its range.
GE Aerospace explains what the T901 is meant to do for U.S. Army rotorcraft.

Preliminary Flight Rating is an airworthiness verdict, not a marketing milestone. It certifies that the engine has demonstrated enough of its performance and safety margins on the ground to be trusted in the air on a developmental aircraft. The Army announced the T901 had passed on 12 August 2026, calling it a key step on the path to full qualification.

GE Aerospace Slumps: Buy the Dip or Avoid?
sum: GE Aerospace (GE +2.76%) remains one of the most intriguing growth stories in the industrial sector, and its recent results helped highlight the case for the stock. If you think share prices reflect a kind of rolling vote on a company's prospects, then the dip is a great buying opportunity, because the company had a lot of good things to say.

I think GE Aerospace is a great company with an exceptional leadership team and a business model (aircraft engines that can be used for more than 40 years, generating a long-term stream of high-margin services revenue) that ensures long-term growth.

However, based on its recently upgraded free cash flow (FCF) guidance of $8.9 billion to $9.2 billion for 2026, investors are going to have to have a pretty solid belief in the company's ability to generate inflation-beating cash flow growth over a long period to justify the current $354 billion market cap.
That said, if you do believe in these fundamentals, then the case for the stock just got stronger. There are three main takeaways from the results.

First, as discussed previously, GE Aerospace's first-quarter earnings report in April was so strong that it was puzzling that management didn't formally raise guidance. The reason came down to uncertainty about the impact of the conflict in Iran on jet fuel prices and, in turn, on flight departures and GE's commercial engine services revenue.

However, commercial engines and services (CES) grew 26% year over year in the second quarter, and CES services orders grew 22% year over year, taking overall CES services orders growth to a whopping 34% in the first half. As such, management now expects its CES services revenue to grow by $5 billion in 2026, up from its April estimate of $4 billion.

Second, the aerospace industry has faced supply chain issues since the pandemic ended, but it appears GE is winning the battle. Not only did management raise expectations for LEAP engine deliveries by a high-teens percentage from a previous estimate of 15%, but CEO Larry Culp also said, "We think about '27 and frankly beyond, it's much more a supply-side challenge than it is demand."
